EQUIPMENT AUCTION BUYER'S PREMIUM CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What will winning this lot actually cost you, out the door?

Enter the hammer price and the auction's own published terms. This stacks the buyer's premium (capped per lot if the auction caps it), the online-bidding premium if you're bidding through their platform, a card surcharge if you're paying by card, sales tax, and a flat doc/title fee — then, if you give it a budget, works backward to the highest hammer price you can bid and stay inside it.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

Just bought the lot to flip it, not to run it? See the storage-auction max-bid calculator for pricing a resale purchase instead.

Selling scrap metal from a salvage lot? The scrap metal yard payout calculator nets a hauled load at two yards after the drive.

Mentally adding a flat percentage instead? See where that usually goes wrong.

Wondering why the tax line is higher than you expected? See why sales tax applies to the buyer's premium, not just the hammer price for a worked example.

What this does and doesn't do

This stacks the buyer's premium (capped per lot if you enter a cap), an online-bidding premium if you check that box, sales tax on the full purchase price unless you mark the purchase exempt, a card surcharge on the whole invoice if you're paying by card, and a flat doc/title fee. It does not know any specific auction house's or state's actual terms — you supply them — and it is not a determination that a specific exemption, cap, or fee applies to your purchase. Treat every number here as a planning estimate to confirm against the auction's own printed terms before you bid.

Common questions

What is a buyer's premium?

A fee the auction house adds on top of your winning (hammer) bid, usually a percentage of it — commonly 10% at farm and heavy-equipment auctions. It is part of what you owe, not included in the hammer price you won at.

Does the buyer's premium cap apply per lot?

Usually yes at equipment auctions — a cap like "$2,500 per lot" limits the premium on each item you win separately, so winning three lots can mean three separate caps, not one shared cap for the whole sale. Always confirm this in the specific auction's own printed terms, since a per-sale or per-day cap works very differently.

Why does bidding online cost more than bidding in person?

Many auctioneers running a live online-bidding platform charge a separate internet or online-bidding premium — commonly 2-3% — for anyone who bids through it, on top of the standard buyer's premium. Bidding from the floor in person usually avoids this extra fee entirely.

Is sales tax charged on the buyer's premium too, or just the hammer price?

Under most published auction terms, sales tax is charged on the full purchase price — the hammer price plus the buyer's premium and any online-bidding premium — not the hammer price alone. Some states or auctioneers only tax the hammer price, and many states exempt qualifying farm equipment entirely, so check the specific auction's terms and your state's rules.

Is this legal, tax, or financial advice?

No. It applies the buyer's premium, fee, and tax terms you enter to a hammer price or budget you supply, as a planning estimate — not a determination of what a specific auction, state, or lender will actually charge. Always confirm the exact terms with the auction house before you bid.

vs-a-flat-percent-rule.html.text:
← back to the calculator

This calculator vs. mentally adding a flat percentage

"Add 10% for the buyer's premium" is close enough for a rough guess and wrong in real money on an actual bid. Equipment auctions stack up to four separate charges on top of the hammer price — a capped premium, an online-bidding premium, a card surcharge, and tax on more than just the hammer price — and a flat mental percentage cannot represent a cap, a conditional fee, or a compounding tax base at the same time.

Where a flat-percentage guess usually goes wrong

ChargeFlat-percentage mistakeWhat this calculator does
Buyer's premium capKeeps applying the percentage past the point where a per-lot cap has already stopped the real charge, overstating the cost on an expensive lot.Charges the lesser of the percentage or the cap you enter, and says on the page when the cap applied.
Online-bidding premiumForgets it entirely, or double-counts it as part of the "buyer's premium" percentage, when it is usually a separate, stacking fee.Adds it only when you say you're bidding online, on top of the buyer's premium, never merged into one number.
Card surchargeApplied to the hammer price alone, if applied at all — when it is normally charged on the whole invoice including every premium and tax.Applies the surcharge to the full invoice total, only when you say you're paying by card.
Sales tax baseTaxes the hammer price only, understating the bill wherever the premium is taxed too — or assumes tax applies when the purchase is actually exempt.Taxes the full purchase price (hammer price plus every premium) unless you mark the purchase exempt, and always discloses which assumption it used.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

Why does a flat percentage overstate the cost on an expensive lot?

Because many equipment auctions cap the buyer's premium per lot — commonly a few thousand dollars — so a flat 10% in your head keeps growing past the point where the cap has already stopped the real bill. On a $45,000 tractor with a $2,500 cap, mentally adding 10% ($4,500) overstates the premium by $2,000.

Why does a flat percentage understate the cost when bidding online?

Because the buyer's premium and the online-bidding (internet) premium are two separate, stacking fees at most houses that run a live online platform. A mental estimate of just the buyer's premium misses the extra 2-3% charged only to bidders using the platform, which a bidder on the floor in person would not owe.

Does a flat percentage account for a card surcharge?

Not unless you remember to add it separately, and it applies to the whole invoice — hammer price, every premium, and tax — not the hammer price alone. Paying by ACH or check instead of a card avoids this fee at houses that charge one.

Is sales tax calculated on the hammer price or the full purchase price?

Under most published auction terms, on the full purchase price — hammer price plus every premium — which a mental estimate that taxes only the hammer price will understate. Some houses or states tax the hammer price alone, and some equipment purchases are exempt entirely, so the specific auction's printed terms are what actually governs, not a general rule.

Does this calculator know my auction's actual terms?

No — you supply the buyer's premium rate and cap, the online and card fees, and the tax rate from the auction's own printed terms. What it removes is the arithmetic mistake of adding them up in the wrong order or forgetting one of them, not the need to read the terms in the first place.

No warranty. This page and the linked calculator apply the buyer's premium, fee, and tax terms you supply. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace confirming the exact terms with the auction house. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. The calculator this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you enter is uploaded anywhere.

why-is-sales-tax-charged-on-the-buyers-p.text:
← back to the calculator

Why is sales tax charged on the buyer's premium, not just the hammer price?

A bidder who mentally taxes the hammer bid and stops there is usually left short at settlement. Under most published auction terms, the "purchase price" that sales tax applies to is the hammer price plus the buyer's premium and any online-bidding premium — the full amount you are actually buying the lot for — not the hammer bid alone.

Open the free equipment auction calculator

Worked example

A $45,000 hammer price, 10% buyer's premium capped at $2,500 per lot, and a 6% sales tax rate:

FigureAmount
Hammer price$45,000.00
Buyer's premium (10%, capped at $2,500)$2,500.00
Taxable purchase price$47,500.00
Sales tax at 6% on the full purchase price$2,850.00
Sales tax at 6% on the hammer price alone (common mistake)$2,700.00
Amount a hammer-price-only estimate understates the tax by$150.00

The $2,500 premium is capped — at an uncapped 10% it would have been $4,500 — and the tax still applies to whatever the premium actually settles at after the cap, not the uncapped figure. The doc/title fee is added after tax, so it is never part of this taxable base either way.

Common questions

Why is sales tax charged on the buyer's premium, not just the hammer price?

Because under most published auction terms, the taxable "purchase price" is defined as everything you owe for the lot before the doc fee — the hammer price plus the buyer's premium and any online-bidding premium — not the hammer bid alone. The premium is part of what you are buying the lot for, so it is part of what gets taxed.

How much does this actually change the bill?

On a $45,000 hammer price with a 10% buyer's premium capped at $2,500, the taxable purchase price is $47,500. At a 6% tax rate that is $2,850 in tax. Taxing the hammer price alone would give $2,700 — $150 less than what the auction actually invoices.

Does the doc or title fee get taxed too?

Not under the common structure this calculator assumes: the doc/title fee is a flat charge added after tax, not part of the taxable purchase price. A card surcharge, where one applies, is charged on the whole invoice including tax and the doc fee — the reverse order from the premium.

Is every auction's tax base the same?

No. A few states or auctioneers tax the hammer price alone, and many states exempt qualifying farm or agricultural equipment from sales tax entirely, usually only for a buyer holding the right exemption certificate. This page describes the common case — always confirm the specific auction's printed terms and your state's rules before you bid.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. Every field on the calculator runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no account, and nothing you type is saved anywhere except in your own browser. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off from the calculator's own page.
